# What this note explains

> **Branch comparison:** this detailed note describes the preserved BRASIL
> baseline. On `rough/operator-based-coefficients`, the live experiments use
> directly computed root/factor coefficients without beta interpolation.
> See the [matched comparison](../docs/rough_operator_comparison.html).
> The result tables and source listings below read the archived baseline,
> so they remain consistent with the mathematical and code explanation.

This note explains the **spatial rough-forcing experiment** in
[original conv_in_h_rough.Rmd](../data_files/rough_comparison/brasil_h_notebook.Rmd). Its implementation is in
[fun/rough](../fun/rough/README.md). It is not an explanation of the separate
temporal rough-forcing experiment.

The differential equation, the data, the finite element method, the rational
update, and the norm used to measure error are all derived here. The code
appendix includes the preserved baseline source, not a rewritten substitute.
Rendering this note reads the saved results and source files. It does not
rerun the forty convergence cases or compile the C++ solver.

There are four objects to keep separate:

| Object | Meaning |
|---|---|
| \(u(t)\) | The solution of the continuous equation with an infinite-series forcing |
| \(u_h(t)\) | The ideal spatial FEM solution, with exact fractional powers and continuous time |
| \(U_{h,m}^k\), and its reconstruction \(U_{h,m}^{\tau}(t)\) | The rational backward Euler FEM approximation actually advanced by the code |
| \(E_{\mathrm{reported}}\) | Its space–time error, evaluated using stable numerical formulas and a bounded remainder of an infinite sum |

The statement \(E_h\asymp h^\alpha/|\log h|\) is first a statement about the
ideal spatial error \(\|u-u_h\|_{L_2(0,T;L_2(\Gamma))}\).
It describes the fully discrete experiment over a range where the other
errors are small. Fixed \(\tau\) and fixed rational order do not give this
asymptotic behavior down to arbitrarily small \(h\).

## Notation

| Symbol | Definition |
|---|---|
| \(\Gamma\) | The tadpole metric graph |
| \(y\in[0,1]\) | Coordinate on the stem; \(y=1\) is the junction |
| \(x\in[0,2]\) | Coordinate on the loop; \(x=0\) and \(x=2\) are the same junction |
| \(L=\kappa^2-\Delta_\Gamma\) | Shifted Kirchhoff–Laplacian |
| \(\beta=\alpha/2\) | Fractional exponent of \(L\) |
| \(\phi_j\), \(j\geq1\) | A selected dyadic family of continuous eigenfunctions |
| \(\mu_j\) | Eigenvalue of \(L\) on \(\phi_j\) |
| \(a_j=\nu\mu_j^\beta\) | Physical decay rate |
| \(J\) | Mesh refinement index; \(h=2^{-J}\) |
| \(n=2^J\) | Number of stem elements |
| \(N\) | Number of time intervals; \(\tau=T/N\) |
| \(C,G,K=\kappa^2C+G\) | FEM mass, stiffness, and shifted stiffness matrices |
| \(B\) | Columns of exact loads of the resolved \(\phi_j\) |
| \(P=C^{-1}B\) | Matrix of their FEM projection coefficients |
| \(\mathsf R_h\) | Gram matrix of their spatial projection residuals |
| \(\mathcal R_m\) | Scalar rational approximation to \(x^{-\beta}\) |
| \(S\) | Signed nodal embedding from a quarter-loop to the full graph |
| \(\Psi v\) | FEM function with coefficient vector \(v\) |

The index \(j\) is **not** the index of the entire ordered graph spectrum.
The functions used here are a sparse, orthonormal subset of that spectrum.

# The graph and the operator

## The metric and the drawing are different things

The graph consists of a stem of length 1 attached to a loop of length 2.
Integration means integration with respect to edge length:
\[
(f,v)_{L_2(\Gamma)}
=\int_0^1 f_{\mathrm{stem}}(y)v_{\mathrm{stem}}(y)\,dy
+\int_0^2 f_{\mathrm{loop}}(x)v_{\mathrm{loop}}(x)\,dx.
\]
The total graph length is 3.

The drawing in `rough_mesh()` uses a straight segment and a polygonal
approximation to a circle of radius \(1/\pi\). A perfect circle of this
radius has circumference 2, but its polygonal approximation has a slightly
different Euclidean length. The code therefore explicitly sets the
**metric** edge lengths to `c(1, 2)`. The differential equation uses those
lengths, not an approximate polygon circumference.

## Domain of the Kirchhoff–Laplacian

The operator acts as a second derivative separately on each edge.
Its domain consists of edgewise \(H^2\) functions satisfying:

1. Continuity at the junction:
   \[
   v_{\mathrm{stem}}(1)=v_{\mathrm{loop}}(0)=v_{\mathrm{loop}}(2).
   \]
2. Neumann condition at the free endpoint:
   \[
   v_{\mathrm{stem}}'(0)=0.
   \]
3. Kirchhoff flux balance at the junction:
   \[
   -v_{\mathrm{stem}}'(1)
   +v_{\mathrm{loop}}'(0)-v_{\mathrm{loop}}'(2)=0.
   \]

The signs come from derivatives directed **outward from the vertex**.
At the right endpoint of an oriented interval the outward derivative is
the negative coordinate derivative. The loop contributes twice at its
junction: once from each endpoint of its interval representation.

Integration by parts with these conditions gives
\[
(-\Delta_\Gamma v,v)=\int_\Gamma |v'|^2.
\]
Thus the shifted operator is positive:
\[
(Lv,v)=\kappa^2\|v\|^2+\|v'\|^2
\geq\kappa^2\|v\|^2.
\]
The positive shift \(\kappa>0\) removes the zero eigenvalue of the unshifted
Kirchhoff–Laplacian and makes inverse fractional powers well-defined.

# Why the selected functions are eigenfunctions

For \(j=1,2,\ldots\), write \(k_j=2^j\), and define
\[
\phi_j=
\begin{cases}
0,&\text{on the stem},\\
\sin(k_j\pi x),&\text{on the loop}.
\end{cases}
\]

## Edgewise differential equation

On the loop,
\[
-\frac{d^2}{dx^2}\sin(k_j\pi x)
=(k_j\pi)^2\sin(k_j\pi x).
\]
On the stem both sides are zero. Therefore, edgewise,
\[
L\phi_j=\left[\kappa^2+(k_j\pi)^2\right]\phi_j.
\]
An edgewise identity alone is not enough: the vertex conditions must also hold.

## Vertex conditions

At the junction,
\[
\phi_{\mathrm{stem}}(1)=0,\qquad
\phi_{\mathrm{loop}}(0)=0,\qquad
\phi_{\mathrm{loop}}(2)=\sin(2k_j\pi)=0.
\]
The free-end Neumann condition holds because the stem function is zero.

At the junction the two loop derivatives are
\[
\phi_{\mathrm{loop}}'(0)=k_j\pi,\qquad
\phi_{\mathrm{loop}}'(2)=k_j\pi\cos(2k_j\pi)=k_j\pi.
\]
Hence the outward derivatives add to
\[
0+k_j\pi-k_j\pi=0.
\]
Each function is smooth on both edges, satisfies all domain conditions,
and is therefore a genuine graph eigenfunction:
\[
\boxed{\mu_j=\kappa^2+\pi^2 2^{2j},\qquad L\phi_j=\mu_j\phi_j.}
\]

The construction would also give loop-supported eigenfunctions
\(\sin(k\pi x)\) for other positive integer \(k\). The dyadic selection
\(k=2^j\) is deliberate: it makes regularity, unresolved loads, tail bounds,
and mesh refinement particularly transparent.

## Normalization and orthogonality

For an integer \(k\geq1\),
\[
\int_0^2\sin^2(k\pi x)\,dx
=\left[\frac{x}{2}-\frac{\sin(2k\pi x)}{4k\pi}\right]_0^2=1.
\]
Thus these functions are already normalized; no extra square-root factor
is required.

For distinct integers \(k,\ell\), the product-to-sum identity gives
\[
\int_0^2\sin(k\pi x)\sin(\ell\pi x)\,dx=0.
\]
The stem contributes zero. Consequently
\[
(\phi_i,\phi_j)_{L_2(\Gamma)}=\delta_{ij}.
\]

This family is not a complete basis of \(L_2(\Gamma)\). However, it can be
included in a full orthonormal eigenbasis, choosing an orthonormal basis
inside each eigenspace if an eigenvalue is repeated. All coefficients of
our data outside this selected family are zero.

# Why the forcing is in \(L_2\), but in no positive spectral Sobolev space

Define the partial sums
\[
g_M=\sum_{j=1}^M\frac1j\phi_j.
\]
Orthogonality gives, for \(M'>M\),
\[
\|g_{M'}-g_M\|_{L_2(\Gamma)}^2
=\sum_{j=M+1}^{M'}\frac1{j^2}\longrightarrow0.
\]
Completeness of \(L_2(\Gamma)\) therefore defines
\[
\boxed{g=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\frac1j\phi_j\quad\text{in }L_2(\Gamma).}
\]
Furthermore,
\[
\|g\|_{L_2(\Gamma)}^2
=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\frac1{j^2}=\frac{\pi^2}{6}.
\]

## The meaning of \(\dot H^s\)

Here the dot denotes a spectral space of the **shifted** operator:
\[
\dot H^s(\Gamma)=D(L^{s/2}),\qquad
\|v\|_{\dot H^s}^2=\sum_\ell \lambda_\ell^s|(v,e_\ell)|^2.
\]
It does not mean a mean-zero subspace. The strictly positive shift makes
this norm nondegenerate, including on constant functions.

The exponent is \(s\), rather than \(2s\), in the weighted sum because the
norm squares \(L^{s/2}\). With the selected eigenfunctions,
\[
\|g\|_{\dot H^s}^2=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\frac{\mu_j^s}{j^2}.
\]
For every \(s>0\),
\[
\frac{\mu_j^s}{j^2}
\geq \pi^{2s}\frac{2^{2sj}}{j^2}\longrightarrow\infty.
\]
The summands do not even tend to zero. Hence
\[
\boxed{g\in L_2(\Gamma),\qquad
g\notin\dot H^s(\Gamma)\ \text{for every }s>0.}
\]

This is why using dyadic frequencies matters. Coefficients \(1/j\) on an
ordinary sequence of frequencies growing only like \(j\) would have some
positive regularity; coefficients \(1/j\) on frequencies growing like
\(2^j\) do not.

## Why choose the coefficient \(1/j\)?

More generally, coefficients \(j^{-p}\) on this dyadic family give an
\(L_2\) forcing when \(p>1/2\), but still give no positive spectral
Sobolev regularity. The corresponding spatial tail has norm of order
\(h^\alpha/J^p\). The choice \(p=1\) is simple, has the familiar norm
\(\sum j^{-2}=\pi^2/6\), and produces the correction factor \(J\).

Setting all coefficients equal to 1 to try to obtain a pure \(h^\alpha\)
tail would make \(\sum_j\|\phi_j\|^2\) diverge. That would no longer be
an \(L_2\) forcing under the assumptions of this experiment. The logarithmic
factor is a feature of these fixed, square-summable data, not an error in
the numerical solver.

## Why the earlier smooth experiment behaved differently

The original matrix experiment uses finite-mode data, namely
\(u_0=10e_5\) and \(f(t)=10\sin(\pi t)e_7\). A finite eigenfunction sum
belongs to every nonnegative-order spectral Sobolev space. The manuscript's
spatial exponent therefore reaches the P1 limit \(2-\epsilon\), regardless
of the tested \(\alpha<2\).

Here the initial condition is zero, so initial regularity imposes no
restriction. The forcing has precisely the \(s_f=0\) regularity needed to
make the forcing term in the estimate select \(\alpha-\epsilon\).
The spatial roughness persists because the forcing is present throughout
the time interval.

## What the series does and does not say pointwise

The definition above is an \(L_2\) definition. It does not require absolute
pointwise convergence, continuity, or existence of vertex values for \(g\).
In particular, one must not differentiate the forcing series term by term
and assume that the differentiated series is an \(L_2\) function.

At a dyadic point \(x=i2^{-J}\), all terms with \(j\geq J\) have zero sine
value. This makes nodal sampling misleading: very high modes can disappear
at every mesh node while still carrying nonzero \(L_2\) energy.
The forcing is assembled through integrals against FEM hats, not through
interpolation of sampled values.

The mean of each selected sine over the loop is zero, so
\(\int_\Gamma g=0\). The solution also has zero graph mean. This is a
property of the chosen data, not the definition of the dotted spaces.

# Deriving and checking the true solution

The physical equation is
\[
u_t+\nu L^\beta u=g,\qquad u(0)=0,\qquad \beta=\alpha/2,\quad\nu>0.
\]
Since the data use only the selected eigenfunctions, seek
\[
u(t)=\sum_{j\geq1}c_j(t)\phi_j.
\]
Taking its inner product with \(\phi_j\) gives
\[
c_j'(t)+a_jc_j(t)=\frac1j,\qquad
c_j(0)=0,\qquad a_j=\nu\mu_j^\beta.
\]
Multiplication by \(e^{a_jt}\) and integration yield
\[
e^{a_jt}c_j(t)=\frac1j\int_0^t e^{a_jr}\,dr,
\]
and therefore
\[
\boxed{
c_j(t)=\frac{1-e^{-a_jt}}{j\,a_j},\qquad
u(t)=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\frac{1-e^{-a_jt}}{j\,a_j}\phi_j.}
\]

## Why the infinite formula really solves the equation

The bound \(0\leq1-e^{-z}\leq\min(z,1)\) gives
\[
|c_j(t)|\leq\min\left(\frac{t}{j},\frac1{j\,a_j}\right).
\]
Thus the solution series converges in \(L_2\), uniformly on bounded time
intervals. Its derivative has coefficients
\[
c_j'(t)=\frac{e^{-a_jt}}j.
\]
These are bounded by the square-summable sequence \(1/j\).
The derivative series is continuous in \(L_2\), including at \(t=0\), by
dominated convergence of the squared coefficients.

Likewise
\[
\nu L^\beta u(t)=\sum_{j\geq1}\frac{1-e^{-a_jt}}j\phi_j
\]
converges in \(L_2\). Adding this series to the derivative series gives
\(g\) coefficient by coefficient. The initial value is zero.
This establishes a strong \(L_2\) solution, rather than only a formal series.

Equivalently, the same function is the semigroup integral
\[
u(t)=\int_0^t e^{-\nu L^\beta(t-r)}g\,dr.
\]
The eigenfunction derivation is the scalar evaluation of this formula.

Uniqueness follows from the energy identity for the difference \(w\) of
two solutions:
\[
\frac12\frac{d}{dt}\|w\|_{L_2}^2
+\nu\|L^{\beta/2}w\|_{L_2}^2=0,\qquad w(0)=0.
\]

## Exact spatial regularity of \(u(t)\)

For every \(t>0\),
\[
\|u(t)\|_{\dot H^\alpha}^2
=\frac1{\nu^2}\sum_{j\geq1}\frac{(1-e^{-a_jt})^2}{j^2}
\leq\frac{\pi^2}{6\nu^2}.
\]
For any \(\delta>0\),
\[
\|u(t)\|_{\dot H^{\alpha+\delta}}^2
=\frac1{\nu^2}\sum_{j\geq1}
\frac{\mu_j^\delta(1-e^{-a_jt})^2}{j^2}=\infty.
\]
Indeed \(a_j\to\infty\), so the parentheses tend to 1, while
\(\mu_j^\delta/j^2\) grows exponentially.

Persistent forcing therefore produces exactly \(\alpha\) orders of spectral
smoothing. It prevents the solution from becoming arbitrarily smooth at
positive times. This differs from a homogeneous equation with rough initial
data, whose high modes decay away.

## Which vertex conditions can be interpreted classically for the solution?

Each \(\phi_j\) belongs to the domain of \(L\), but an infinite sum of such
functions need not belong to that domain. For every \(t>0\) and
\(\alpha<2\), the regularity calculation above gives
\(u(t)\notin\dot H^2=D(L)\). The equation uses \(L^{\alpha/2}u\), defined
spectrally, rather than requiring \(Lu\) to exist in \(L_2\).

For these particular data, the solution is nevertheless continuous on the
graph for every \(\alpha>0\):
\[
\sum_{j\geq1}|c_j(t)|\|\phi_j\|_\infty
\leq C\sum_{j\geq1}\frac{2^{-\alpha j}}j<\infty.
\]
The uniform convergence preserves the zero junction values and zero stem.

When \(\alpha>1\), the derivative series also converges uniformly because
\[
\sum_{j\geq1}2^j\pi|c_j(t)|
\leq C\sum_{j\geq1}\frac{2^{(1-\alpha)j}}j<\infty.
\]
In this range the two loop endpoint derivatives are equal and the
Kirchhoff derivative balance can be read classically, even though the
second derivatives are not square-integrable.

For \(0<\alpha\leq1\), one should not impose a classical finite derivative
at the junction on this solution. This is not merely a failure to justify
termwise differentiation. Along \(x_n=2^{-n}\), all modes \(j\geq n\)
vanish, while the remaining sine arguments lie in \([0,\pi/2]\).
Using \(\sin z\geq2z/\pi\) on that interval and
\(1-e^{-a_jt}\geq1/2\) for all sufficiently large \(j\), one obtains
\[
\frac{u(x_n,t)}{x_n}
\geq C\sum_{j=j_0}^{n-1}\frac{2^{(1-\alpha)j}}j\longrightarrow\infty.
\]
Thus the finite one-sided loop derivative fails at the junction in that
range. The spectral fractional equation is still well-defined and the
solution still satisfies it strongly in \(L_2\). The Kirchhoff conditions
define the underlying operator and its eigenfunctions; they do not imply
that every element of every fractional domain has classical derivative traces.

# Uniform dyadic meshes and FEM matrices

## Why \(h=2^{-J}\)

Set \(n=2^J\), so \(h=1/n\). Then the stem has \(n\) elements and the loop
has \(2n\) elements of exactly the same physical length.

This choice provides four useful facts:

1. Both edge lengths are integer multiples of \(h\).
2. The mesh nodes align with the dyadic sine frequencies.
3. All unresolved sine loads vanish exactly, with a precisely known cutoff.
4. The four signed quarter-loop copies align node by node.

The experiment uses \(J=5,6,7,8,9\), namely
\(h=1/32,1/64,1/128,1/256,1/512\).
A general unaligned mesh is possible, but its unresolved loads would not
have the exact vanishing property used by this implementation.

## Node counts and data structures

The stem has \(n+1\) distinct nodes. The loop adds \(2n-1\) interior nodes,
because its two endpoint coordinates are one existing junction node.
Thus the full FEM dimension is
\[
N_h=(n+1)+(2n-1)=3n.
\]

In the graph representation used by `rough_mesh()`:

- Node 1 is the free endpoint and node 2 is the junction.
- A row of `graph$mesh$PtE` gives an edge number and a relative edge coordinate.
- Interior row \(r\) corresponds to global node \(2+r\).
- Relative loop coordinates are multiplied by 2 to get physical \(x\).
- `loop_nodes` starts and ends with global node 2. This repeats a reference
  to the same node; it does not create a second junction.

The code checks both the dimension \(3n\) and the actual element lengths.

## Local and global matrices

Let \(\{\psi_i\}\) be the continuous piecewise linear nodal basis and write
\(v_h=\Psi v=\sum_i v_i\psi_i\). The local matrices on an element of length \(h\) are
\[
C_e=\frac h6
\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix},\qquad
G_e=\frac1h
\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Assembly adds contributions at shared nodes, including both sides of the
loop junction. Globally,
\[
C_{ij}=(\psi_j,\psi_i),\qquad
G_{ij}=(\psi_j',\psi_i'),\qquad K=\kappa^2C+G.
\]
The code uses the **consistent** mass matrix \(C\); it does not lump it.

The coefficient matrix of the discrete operator \(L_h\) is
\[
A_h=C^{-1}K.
\]
It is self-adjoint in the mass inner product
\((v,w)_C=v^\mathsf TCw\), although generally not symmetric in the ordinary
Euclidean inner product. The symmetric matrix \(K\) alone is not the
coefficient representation of \(L_h\).

For example,
\[
\|\Psi v\|_{L_2(\Gamma)}^2=v^\mathsf TCv.
\]
Using an ordinary vector norm here would measure a different quantity.

# Exact sine–hat loads and the disappearance of unresolved modes

## Derivation of the sine–hat integral

For a periodic loop hat centered at \(x_i\), let
\[
\psi_i(x_i+r)=1-|r|/h,\qquad |r|\leq h.
\]
For a sine of frequency \(w\), oddness eliminates one term:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int \sin(wx)\psi_i(x)\,dx
&=\sin(wx_i)\,2\int_0^h(1-r/h)\cos(wr)\,dr\\
&=\sin(wx_i)\,\frac{2(1-\cos(wh))}{h w^2}\\
&=h\,\operatorname{sinc}^2(wh/2)\sin(wx_i),
\end{aligned}
\]
where \(\operatorname{sinc}(z)=\sin(z)/z\), with value 1 at zero.

For mode \(j\), set
\[
\theta_j=\pi 2^j h.
\]
Then the load column \(B_j\) is exactly
\[
(B_j)_i=h\,\operatorname{sinc}^2(\theta_j/2)\sin(2^j\pi x_i)
\]
at interior loop nodes, and zero on stem nodes.

At the junction the loop hat has one piece near \(x=0\) and another near
\(x=2\). The sine changes sign under wrapping across the junction.
The two integrals cancel. The junction load is therefore also zero.

## Why modes \(j\geq J\) have zero loads

At a loop node \(x_i=ih=i2^{-J}\),
\[
\sin(2^j\pi x_i)=\sin(\pi i2^{j-J})=0\qquad(j\geq J).
\]
The integral formula, together with the junction cancellation, proves
\[
(\phi_j,\psi_i)=0\quad\text{for every hat }\psi_i,\qquad j\geq J.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{P_h\phi_j=0\quad(j\geq J).}
\]

The proof uses the hat integral. Zero nodal samples by themselves would
not imply zero loads for an arbitrary function.

For \(j<J\), \(\theta_j\leq\pi/2\), so the highest retained sine has four
elements per wavelength. The code assembles precisely
\(j=1,\ldots,J-1\), using `sinpi(x*k)` to evaluate \(\sin(\pi xk)\) with
better argument reduction near integer arguments.

## Why the finite load still represents the infinite forcing

The functional \(v\mapsto(v,\psi_i)\) is continuous on \(L_2\), so the
definition of \(g\) permits
\[
(g,\psi_i)=\lim_{M\to\infty}\sum_{j=1}^M\frac1j(\phi_j,\psi_i)
=\sum_{j=1}^{J-1}\frac1j(B_j)_i.
\]
Consequently the exact full forcing load is
\[
\boxed{b=B(1,1/2,\ldots,1/(J-1))^\mathsf T.}
\]

The code line `load <- as.numeric(B %*% (1/j))` is thus an exact finite
representation of the load of the **fixed infinite** \(g\).
It is not the choice of a different finite forcing for each mesh.

# Orthogonal projection and its stable residual Gram matrix

For a function \(\phi\), its \(L_2\)-orthogonal FEM projection satisfies
\[
(P_h\phi,\psi_i)=(\phi,\psi_i).
\]
If its coefficient vector is \(p\), then \(Cp=b(\phi)\). For all resolved
modes together,
\[
\boxed{CP=B,\qquad P=C^{-1}B.}
\]
The matrix \(P\) has \(N_h\) rows and \(J-1\) columns.

Let \(r_j=\phi_j-P_h\phi_j\) and define
\[
(\mathsf R_h)_{ij}=(r_i,r_j).
\]
Orthogonality of the projection gives the exact identity
\[
\boxed{\mathsf R_h=I-P^\mathsf TCP=I-B^\mathsf TC^{-1}B.}
\]
This matrix is positive semidefinite.

## Why the code does not subtract these matrices

For a well-resolved smooth sine, \(\|r_j\|^2\) is very small.
Computing it as \(1-\|P_h\phi_j\|^2\) subtracts numbers close to 1 and can
lose most relative accuracy or produce a tiny negative result.

`rough_projection()` instead evaluates the residual function itself on
each element:
\[
r_j(x_{\ell}+hz)
=\sin(2^j\pi(x_\ell+hz))
-\big[(1-z)P_{\ell j}+zP_{\ell+1,j}\big].
\]
It integrates products \(r_i r_j\) with a 16-point Gauss–Legendre rule,
summing over loop elements and also over stem elements. The latter terms
include any floating-point leakage of the computed projection onto the stem.

The reference interval transformation is
\[
z=(\xi+1)/2,\qquad dx=h\,dz,
\]
so the weights are the standard Gauss weights divided by 2, then multiplied
by \(h\).

This is stable spatial quadrature, not a symbolic exact integration of
sine products. The residual is not a polynomial. The order is sufficient
for the retained frequencies and was checked by doubling it to 32.
The resulting Gram matrix is assembled as a sum of weighted cross-products,
which preserves positivity much better than subtraction.

# The matrix backward Euler method

With \(u_0=0\) and a constant forcing, the ideal spatial FEM equation is
\[
u_h'(t)+\nu L_h^\beta u_h(t)=P_hg,\qquad u_h(0)=0.
\]
Write the coefficient vector at step \(k\) as \(U^k\).
Backward Euler gives
\[
\big[I+\tau\nu(C^{-1}K)^\beta\big]U^{k+1}
=U^k+\tau C^{-1}b.
\]
There is no sine-in-time forcing average in this experiment: the forcing
is constant, so its interval average is exactly itself.

## Normalize the operator

Put
\[
X=C^{-1}K/\kappa^2,\qquad
s=\tau\nu\kappa^{2\beta}.
\]
The eigenvalues of \(X\) are at least 1. The exact one-step function is
\[
H_{\mathrm{exact}}(x)=\frac1{1+s x^\beta}
=\frac{x^{-\beta}}{x^{-\beta}+s}.
\]
Thus the normalized inverse power is the object approximated rationally.

The code obtains
\[
\mathcal R_m(x)=k_0+\sum_{\ell=1}^m\frac{r_\ell}{x-p_\ell}
\approx x^{-\beta},
\qquad p_\ell<0,\quad r_\ell>0,\quad k_0\geq0.
\]
It uses BRASIL coefficient tables in `rSPDE`.
The table column called `alpha` is evaluated at **\(\beta=\alpha/2\)**,
not at the PDE order \(\alpha\).

The published experiment explicitly uses order 14, with a table row at
each requested \(\beta\). The helper defaults still say `order = 16L`;
the experiment overrides them. Calling a low-level helper without this
override is not a reproduction of the published settings. In particular,
some higher-order table rows have a negative constant and are rejected by
the positivity checks.

## The rational evolution function

Replace \(x^{-\beta}\) by \(\mathcal R_m(x)\):
\[
\boxed{H_m(x)=\frac{\mathcal R_m(x)}{\mathcal R_m(x)+s}.}
\]
For \(x\geq1\), positivity gives \(0<H_m(x)<1\).
This explains stability in the mass norm: every scalar spectral multiplier
of the discrete self-adjoint operator lies between 0 and 1.

The exact scalar transfer error is
\[
H_m(x)-H_{\mathrm{exact}}(x)
=\frac{s(\mathcal R_m(x)-x^{-\beta})}
{(\mathcal R_m(x)+s)(x^{-\beta}+s)}.
\]
It is the inverse-approximation error propagated through the backward Euler
resolvent. A fixed degree does not control this error uniformly over
arbitrarily fine meshes merely because it worked on the current range.

# Why the partial fractions have the form used in the code

## Location and uniqueness of the new poles

Sort the original poles:
\[
p_1<\cdots<p_m<0.
\]
The new poles \(z_\ell\) solve
\[
\mathcal R_m(z_\ell)+s=0.
\]
Between original poles,
\[
\mathcal R_m'(x)=-\sum_{\ell=1}^m\frac{r_\ell}{(x-p_\ell)^2}<0.
\]
On each interval \((p_i,p_{i+1})\), the function decreases from \(+\infty\)
to \(-\infty\), so there is exactly one root.
There is also exactly one root in \((-\infty,p_1)\): the limit of
\(\mathcal R_m+s\) at \(-\infty\) is \(k_0+s>0\), while its left-hand limit
at \(p_1\) is \(-\infty\).
There are no roots to the right of \(p_m\), where the function is positive.

Hence there are exactly \(m\) new poles, all negative.

`rough_transfer()` brackets the first root by repeatedly doubling a
negative left endpoint until the sign is correct. Each interval is mapped
to \(z\in[0,1]\) before calling `uniroot()`. The normalized coordinate
avoids using one absolute tolerance for poles on very different scales.
At an original pole the code supplies the appropriate very large signed
endpoint value instead of evaluating a division by zero.

## Residues and the constant term

At a new pole \(z_\ell\), \(\mathcal R_m(z_\ell)=-s\), so
\[
w_\ell
=\frac{\mathcal R_m(z_\ell)}{\mathcal R_m'(z_\ell)}
=\frac{s}{\sum_i r_i/(z_\ell-p_i)^2}>0.
\]
Also
\[
d=\lim_{x\to\infty}H_m(x)=\frac{k_0}{k_0+s}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{H_m(x)=d+\sum_{\ell=1}^m\frac{w_\ell}{x-z_\ell}.}
\]

The code's `residues` after this transformation are the \(w_\ell\), not the
original \(r_\ell\). Its `remainder` is \(d\).
Dropping \(d\) would implement a different one-step function.

The reconstruction check evaluates both formulas at 257 logarithmically
spaced points from 1 to \(10^{10}\), requiring maximum absolute discrepancy
at most \(2\times10^{-12}\). This checks the partial-fraction conversion.
It is not a proof of rational approximation accuracy over the whole real axis.

## Conversion to sparse FEM systems

Let \(q=C U^k+\tau b\). Since
\[
X-zI=C^{-1}(K/\kappa^2-zC),
\]
we have
\[
(X-zI)^{-1}C^{-1}=(K/\kappa^2-zC)^{-1}.
\]
The coefficient update becomes
\[
\boxed{
U^{k+1}
=d\,C^{-1}q+
\sum_{\ell=1}^m w_\ell
(K/\kappa^2-z_\ell C)^{-1}q.}
\]
Every shifted matrix is symmetric positive definite because
\(K/\kappa^2\) and \(C\) are positive definite and \(z_\ell<0\).

The matrices are fixed for a complete case \((h,\alpha,\tau,m,\nu)\).
They are factored once and solved against a new right-hand side at every
time step. No discrete eigenvectors are required.

The R object stores `m = length(A)-1L` for compatibility with the original
`my.solver.frac()` loop, which executes `m+1` solves. This internal field
is therefore 13 for the order-14 representation. The published rational
order remains 14. The C++ variable `m` is instead the actual residue count, 14.

# Exact quarter-loop symmetry reduction

## The four signed copies

For every selected frequency \(k=2^j\), \(k\) is even, and
\[
\sin(k\pi(1-x))=-\sin(k\pi x),\quad
\sin(k\pi(1+x))=\sin(k\pi x),\quad
\sin(k\pi(2-x))=-\sin(k\pi x).
\]
The values at \(0,1/2,1,3/2,2\) are zero.
Thus values on \(0<x<1/2\) determine the full loop through four signed copies.
The stem remains zero.

The quarter-loop has \(n/2-1\) interior unknowns. For a quarter-loop grid
index \(r=1,\ldots,n/2-1\), the corresponding full loop grid indices are
\[
r,\quad n-r,\quad n+r,\quad 2n-r
\]
with signs \(+,-,+,-\).
`rough_symmetry_embedding()` places exactly these four entries in each
column of the sparse matrix \(S\).

In exact arithmetic,
\[
S^\mathsf TS=4I.
\]
At \(J=9\), the full graph has 1536 unknowns; the reduced system has 255.

## Why this is the same FEM evolution

This reduction uses a nodal symmetry, not a truncated eigenfunction basis.
Uniform mass and stiffness stencils preserve the signed pattern, including
cancellation at its zero boundary nodes. Both \(C\) and \(K\) leave the
coefficient subspace \(\operatorname{range}(S)\) invariant. The exact load
also lies in that subspace.

Restrict the matrices and load by
\[
C_r=S^\mathsf TCS,\qquad
K_r=S^\mathsf TKS,\qquad b_r=S^\mathsf Tb.
\]
The projected continuum basis is obtained from
\[
C_rP_r=S^\mathsf TB,\qquad SP_r=P.
\]
The code checks the last equality numerically.

For any right-hand side generated by this evolution, the full shifted
solution lies in \(\operatorname{range}(S)\). Multiplying the full equation
by \(S^\mathsf T\) gives the restricted equation, and lifting its unique
solution by \(S\) recovers the full solution. This holds for the mass solve
and every rational shifted solve, hence inductively at every time step.

Furthermore,
\[
\|\Psi S v\|_{L_2(\Gamma)}^2=v^\mathsf TC_rv.
\]
No factor of 4 is missing: the four copies have already been included by
the products \(S^\mathsf TCS\) and \(S^\mathsf TKS\).
The residual Gram matrix remains the full-graph \(\mathsf R_h\).

This equivalence requires this forcing, the zero initial condition, and
the aligned uniform mesh. It must not be assumed for arbitrary data.
Setting `symmetry_reduction = FALSE` runs the full matrix system for comparison.

# The exact space–time error identity

The reconstruction is right-constant:
\[
U_{h,m}^\tau(t)=\Psi U^k,\qquad t\in(t_{k-1},t_k].
\]
Its value at the isolated point \(t=0\) does not affect an \(L_2\) norm.

Separate the exact solution into
\[
u(t)=\sum_{j<J}c_j(t)\phi_j+\sum_{j\geq J}c_j(t)\phi_j.
\]
Every high mode is orthogonal to the entire FEM space, and also to the
resolved continuum modes. Therefore the squared error is a sum of two
noninteracting nonnegative contributions:
\[
E^2=E_{\mathrm{resolved}}^2+E_{\mathrm{tail}}^2.
\]

## Resolved spatial identity at a fixed time

Write \(c(t)=(c_1(t),\ldots,c_{J-1}(t))^\mathsf T\).
Orthogonal projection gives
\[
\boxed{
\left\|\sum_{j<J}c_j(t)\phi_j-\Psi U^k\right\|^2
=(U^k-Pc(t))^\mathsf TC(U^k-Pc(t))
+c(t)^\mathsf T\mathsf R_hc(t).}
\]
This form is a sum of squared norms. It avoids evaluating the cancellation-prone
expression \(\|u\|^2+\|U\|^2-2(u,U)\).

## Integrating one interval using moments

Let
\[
\bar c_k=\frac1\tau\int_{t_{k-1}}^{t_k}c(t)\,dt,\qquad
\Sigma_k=\int_{t_{k-1}}^{t_k}(c-\bar c_k)(c-\bar c_k)^\mathsf T\,dt.
\]
Expanding around the mean eliminates all terms linear in \(c-\bar c_k\).
The interval contribution is
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\tau(U^k-P\bar c_k)^\mathsf TC(U^k-P\bar c_k)
+\tau\bar c_k^\mathsf T\mathsf R_h\bar c_k\\
&\hspace{1cm}
+\operatorname{tr}\big((P^\mathsf TCP+\mathsf R_h)\Sigma_k\big).
\end{aligned}
\]
Because \(P^\mathsf TCP+\mathsf R_h=I\), this reduces to
\[
\boxed{
E_{\mathrm{resolved}}^2
=\sum_{k=1}^N\tau\left[
\delta_k^\mathsf TC\delta_k+
\bar c_k^\mathsf T\mathsf R_h\bar c_k+
\sum_{j<J}v_{j,k}
\right],}
\]
where \(\delta_k=U^k-P\bar c_k\) and
\[
v_{j,k}=\frac1\tau\int_{t_{k-1}}^{t_k}(c_j(t)-\bar c_{j,k})^2\,dt.
\]

There is no assumption that different coefficient functions are uncorrelated
in time. Their cross-covariances disappear because the continuum spatial
Gram matrix is the identity. This is why the code needs only `variance_sum`.

The reduced implementation replaces \(U^k,P,C\) by their restricted
counterparts in the first term. The identity remains the same.

# Stable formulas for the time moments

Put
\[
d_j=\frac1{j a_j},\qquad t_0=t_{k-1},\qquad z_j=a_j\tau,\qquad
\omega(z)=\frac{1-e^{-z}}z,\quad\omega(0)=1.
\]
A direct integration gives
\[
\bar c_{j,k}=d_j[1-e^{-a_jt_0}\omega(z_j)].
\]
The code evaluates the equivalent expression
\[
\boxed{\bar c_{j,k}
=d_j\left[-\operatorname{expm1}(-a_jt_0)
+e^{-a_jt_0}(1-\omega(z_j))\right].}
\]
Here `expm1(x)` computes \(e^x-1\) accurately even when \(x\) is tiny.

## The function one_minus_average()

Directly subtracting \(\omega(z)\) from 1 loses relative accuracy for
small \(z\). The series is
\[
1-\omega(z)=\frac z2-\frac{z^2}{6}+\frac{z^3}{24}
-\frac{z^4}{120}+\cdots
=\sum_{r=1}^\infty\frac{(-1)^{r+1}z^r}{(r+1)!}.
\]
For \(z<0.05\), the C++ function starts with \(z/2\) and applies the recurrence
\[
\mathrm{term}_r=\mathrm{term}_{r-1}\frac{-z}{r+1}
\]
through degree 16. For larger \(z\), it uses
\(1+\operatorname{expm1}(-z)/z\).

## The function exponential_variance()

The interval variance is
\[
v_{j,k}=d_j^2e^{-2a_jt_0}V(z_j),\qquad
V(z)=\omega(2z)-\omega(z)^2.
\]
As \(z\to0\),
\[
V(z)=\frac{z^2}{12}-\frac{z^3}{12}
+\frac{17z^4}{360}+O(z^5).
\]
The direct formula subtracts two values close to 1, although the result
is only of size \(z^2\).

For \(z\geq0.05\), the C++ function evaluates that formula using `expm1`.
For smaller \(z\), it uses the positive centered integral
\[
V(z)=\int_0^1
\left[\operatorname{expm1}(-z\xi)+(1-\omega(z))\right]^2\,d\xi
\]
with an eight-point Gauss–Legendre rule. The centered integrand retains
the small deviations accurately.

Thus the **moment identity** is exact in real arithmetic, while the
small-argument variance branch is a very accurate numerical quadrature.
It should not be described as symbolic exact integration at every machine
operation. This branch, and the spatial residual quadrature, were checked
independently.

# The unresolved series and its remainder

Since the selected eigenfunctions are orthonormal,
\[
E_{\mathrm{tail}}^2
=\sum_{j=J}^{\infty}\frac{F(a_j,T)}{j^2a_j^2},
\qquad
F(a,T)=\int_0^T(1-e^{-at})^2\,dt.
\]
Expanding the square and integrating yields
\[
\boxed{
F(a,T)=T-\frac{2(1-e^{-aT})}{a}
+\frac{1-e^{-2aT}}{2a}.}
\]

## Stable evaluation of \(F\)

Let \(z=aT\). The formula becomes
\[
F(a,T)=T\left[
1+\frac{2\operatorname{expm1}(-z)}z
-\frac{\operatorname{expm1}(-2z)}{2z}
\right].
\]
Even this expression cancels for small \(z\), so `rough_response_integral()`
uses, for \(z<0.1\),
\[
F(a,T)
=T\sum_{r=2}^{18}\frac{(-1)^r(2^r-2)z^r}{(r+1)!}
\]
as a truncated Taylor evaluation. The leading terms are
\[
F(a,T)=T\left(\frac{z^2}{3}-\frac{z^3}{4}
+\frac{7z^4}{60}+\cdots\right).
\]
They agree with \(1-e^{-at}\approx at\), which gives \(a^2T^3/3\).

The function returns \(F\), not \(F/a^2\). The caller divides by
\((j a_j)^2\) exactly once.

## Bounding every term beyond a stopping index

Because \(F(a,T)\leq T\) and
\[
a_j\geq\nu\pi^\alpha2^{\alpha j},
\]
after summing through \(M\) the remaining squared tail satisfies
\[
\begin{aligned}
0\leq\sum_{j=M+1}^{\infty}\frac{F(a_j,T)}{j^2a_j^2}
&\leq
\frac{T}{\nu^2\pi^{2\alpha}}
\sum_{j=M+1}^{\infty}\frac{2^{-2\alpha j}}{j^2}\\
&\leq
\boxed{\frac{T}{\nu^2\pi^{2\alpha}}
\frac{2^{-2\alpha(M+1)}}{(M+1)^2(1-2^{-2\alpha})}.}
\end{aligned}
\]
The second inequality replaces each \(1/j^2\) by \(1/(M+1)^2\), then sums
a geometric series.

The loop stops when this bound is at most `relative_tolerance` times the
accumulated squared tail. The default is \(10^{-13}\). It returns:

- `squared`: the accumulated squared tail;
- `omitted_squared_bound`: the upper bound above;
- `last_j`: the last summed index.

The loop limit 450 is a failure guard. If the tolerance has not been met,
the function stops with an error. It does not silently redefine the
forcing as a 450-mode forcing.

The bound is a mathematical real-arithmetic truncation bound. The summation
does not use outward-rounded interval arithmetic, so it is not by itself
a rigorous bound on every floating-point rounding error.

If the accumulated total squared error is \(A\) and the omitted tail is
bounded by \(B\), then, ignoring the other numerical evaluation errors,
\[
\sqrt A\leq E\leq\sqrt{A+B},\qquad
\sqrt{A+B}-\sqrt A
=\frac{B}{\sqrt{A+B}+\sqrt A}\leq\frac{B}{2\sqrt A}.
\]
This converts a squared-tail bound into a bound on the reported norm.

# Why the spatial error has order \(h^\alpha/J\)

This section derives the ideal spatial rate, not merely an upper bound
obtained by assigning regularity indices to a theorem.

## Lower bound from modes invisible to every FEM function

For any \(V_h\)-valued approximation, including the numerical time-stepping
solution,
\[
\|u-U_h\|_{L_2(0,T;L_2)}^2\geq E_{\mathrm{tail}}^2.
\]
For fixed \(\nu,T>0\), \(a_JT\to\infty\) as \(J\to\infty\).
Once \(a_JT\) is sufficiently large, \(F(a_j,T)\) is bounded above and below
by positive constants times \(T\), uniformly for \(j\geq J\).
Also \(a_j\asymp2^{\alpha j}\), with constants depending on \(\nu,\kappa,\alpha\).

Consequently
\[
E_{\mathrm{tail}}^2
\asymp\sum_{j\geq J}\frac{2^{-2\alpha j}}{j^2}
\asymp\frac{2^{-2\alpha J}}{J^2}.
\]
For the lower inequality it suffices to retain the \(j=J\) term.
For the upper inequality use \(j^{-2}\leq J^{-2}\) and a geometric sum.
Thus no FEM approximation can have an error smaller in order than
\(h^\alpha/J\) for these data.

## The resolved-mode FEM identities

These identities are used in the mathematical analysis and the independent
oracle. The production solver does not use them to advance \(U^k\).

Let \(I_h\phi_j\) denote the nodal interpolant of a retained sine.
Set
\[
\theta=\pi2^j h,\qquad
\rho(\theta)=\frac{2+\cos\theta}{3},\qquad
\sigma(\theta)=\frac{\sin(\theta/2)}{\theta/2}.
\]
The uniform mass and stiffness stencils applied to its nodal sine vector give
\[
C(I_h\phi_j)=h\rho(\theta)(I_h\phi_j),\qquad
G(I_h\phi_j)=\frac{4\sin^2(\theta/2)}h(I_h\phi_j),
\]
where these expressions refer to coefficient vectors at interior loop nodes;
the junction and zero stem rows satisfy the same eigenvector identity.

Hence its generalized eigenvalue is
\[
\boxed{
\mu_{j,h}=\kappa^2+
\frac{12\sin^2(\theta/2)}{h^2(2+\cos\theta)}.}
\]
Since the exact sine–hat load has the factor \(h\sigma^2\),
\[
P_h\phi_j=\frac{\sigma^2}{\rho}I_h\phi_j.
\]
Discrete sine orthogonality gives \(\|I_h\phi_j\|^2=\rho\), so
\[
\gamma_j:=\|P_h\phi_j\|^2=\frac{\sigma^4}{\rho},\qquad
\|\phi_j-P_h\phi_j\|^2=1-\gamma_j.
\]
Taylor expansion gives
\[
1-\gamma_j=\frac{\theta^4}{720}+O(\theta^6),\qquad
\frac{|\mu_{j,h}-\mu_j|}{\mu_j}\leq C\theta^2
\quad(0<\theta\leq\pi/2).
\]
Thus the \(L_2\) projection error is of size \(\theta^2\), not \(\theta^4\);
the latter is its squared norm.

## Upper bound for the ideal spatial evolution

Define
\[
q(a,t)=\frac{1-e^{-at}}a,\qquad
a_{j,h}=\nu\mu_{j,h}^{\alpha/2}.
\]
The ideal spatial FEM solution is
\[
u_h(t)=\sum_{j<J}\frac1j q(a_{j,h},t)P_h\phi_j.
\]
The retained projected sine modes are mutually orthogonal in the mass norm.
Projection orthogonality then gives the exact resolved-mode error
\[
\frac1{j^2}\left[
(1-\gamma_j)\int_0^Tq(a_j,t)^2\,dt+
\gamma_j\int_0^T(q(a_j,t)-q(a_{j,h},t))^2\,dt
\right].
\]

We have \(|q(a,t)|\leq1/a\) and
\[
|\partial_aq(a,t)|
=\left|\int_0^t-r e^{-ar}\,dr\right|\leq a^{-2}.
\]
The discrete and continuous rates are comparable, with relative difference
\(O(\theta^2)\). Both resolved error contributions are therefore bounded by
\(C\theta^4/(j^2a_j^2)\). Summing gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\|u-u_h\|_{L_2(0,T;L_2)}^2
&\leq C\left[
h^4\sum_{j=1}^{J-1}\frac{2^{(4-2\alpha)j}}{j^2}
+\sum_{j\geq J}\frac{2^{-2\alpha j}}{j^2}\right].
\end{aligned}
\]

For \(0<\alpha<2\), \(b=2^{4-2\alpha}>1\), and
\[
\sum_{j<J}\frac{b^j}{j^2}\leq C_b\frac{b^J}{J^2}.
\]
One proof splits the sum at \(J/2\). Above \(J/2\), use
\(j^{-2}\leq4/J^2\) and a geometric sum. Below \(J/2\), the exponential
factor is at most \(b^{J/2}\), which is eventually dominated by \(b^J/J^2\).
A larger constant handles the finitely many small \(J\).

Since \(h=2^{-J}\),
\[
h^4\frac{2^{(4-2\alpha)J}}{J^2}
=\frac{h^{2\alpha}}{J^2}.
\]
Combining upper and lower bounds proves
\[
\boxed{
\|u-u_h\|_{L_2(0,T;L_2(\Gamma))}
\asymp\frac{h^\alpha}{J}
=\frac{(\log2)h^\alpha}{|\log h|},
\qquad0<\alpha<2.}
\]

## A stronger limit, and why an order bound alone is not a slope proof

Two-sided bounds \(\asymp\) alone do not guarantee convergence of successive
log-log slopes. For this particular uniform dyadic construction, the modal
formula also gives a positive limiting constant.

To see its structure, write \(j=J+r\) and set
\[
\theta_r=\pi2^r,\qquad
F_r=\frac{12\sin^2(\theta_r/2)}
{\theta_r^2(2+\cos\theta_r)},\qquad
\gamma_r=\frac{3[\sin(\theta_r/2)/(\theta_r/2)]^4}{2+\cos\theta_r}.
\]
For \(r<0\), define
\[
A_r=1-\gamma_r+\gamma_r(1-F_r^{-\alpha/2})^2.
\]
For fixed \(r\), as \(J\to\infty\), the shift becomes negligible relative
to the frequency, both modal rates become large, the transient portion of
the time integral vanishes, and \(J/j\to1\).
The scaled squared error converges to
\[
\boxed{
C_\alpha^2=
\frac{T}{\nu^2\pi^{2\alpha}}
\left[\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}2^{-2\alpha r}
+\sum_{r=-\infty}^{-1}2^{-2\alpha r}A_r\right]>0.}
\]
For negative \(r\), \(A_r=O(2^{4r})\), so the second sum converges precisely
when \(\alpha<2\). The same geometric estimates used in the upper bound
control the summation tails; contributions of fixed low modes vanish under
this scaling. These bounds justify passing to the limit.

Thus the ideal spatial error satisfies the stronger relation
\[
\|u-u_h\|_{L_2(0,T;L_2)}
\sim C_\alpha\,h^\alpha/J.
\]
This explains the asymptotic slope model.

## Why \(\alpha=2\) is different, and why \(\alpha=1.9\) is difficult

At \(\alpha=2\), the resolved upper sum becomes
\[
h^4\sum_{j<J}\frac1{j^2}=O(h^4),
\]
whereas the unresolved squared tail is only \(O(h^4/J^2)\).
A fixed low mode supplies an \(h^2\) spatial error, so the dominant spatial
behavior is second order. The formula \(h^2/J\) is not the correct dominant
error at this endpoint.

As \(\alpha\) approaches 2 from below, the geometric ratio
\(2^{4-2\alpha}\) approaches 1. Convergence toward the limiting
\(h^\alpha/J\) regime becomes slow, and low-mode second-order terms remain
important over practical meshes. The code intentionally requires
\(0<\alpha<2\); it is not an endpoint implementation.

# Slopes, finite ranges, and the theorem in the manuscript

## Raw and logarithmically corrected slopes

For the leading model,
\[
E_J=C\,2^{-\alpha J}/J,
\]
the successive raw slope is
\[
\log_2(E_J/E_{J+1})
=\alpha+\log_2((J+1)/J).
\]
It exceeds \(\alpha\). The local derivative of the log-log model is
\(\alpha+1/(J\log2)\).

Multiplying by \(J\) removes the leading logarithmic factor:
\[
J E_J\sim C h^\alpha.
\]
This is why the second plot uses \(J E\), rather than \(E\), on its vertical axis.

The regression uses the three finest meshes \(J=7,8,9\). Since regression
is linear in the dependent variable, adding \(\log J\) shifts every fitted
slope by the same quantity, independent of the numerical errors or of \(\alpha\):
\[
s_{\mathrm{corrected}}
=s_{\mathrm{raw}}
+\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(\log h,\log J)}
{\operatorname{Var}(\log h)}.
\]
The correction is about \(-0.181285\) for this fit range. It is a prescribed
model correction, not a procedure that is guaranteed to move every finite-range
slope closer to \(\alpha\).

In particular, the \(\alpha=1.9\) raw slope is about 1.9700, while its
corrected slope is about 1.7887. The corrected value is farther from 1.9
on this range. This is consistent with slow preasymptotic behavior near
second order, rather than evidence that either number is an exact
asymptotic exponent.

## Connection with the manuscript estimate

The theorem is `lastlasttheorem` in
[main.tex](../../6ac76d140751a76e98ae4d0b/main.tex). Its spatial exponent is
\[
p=\min\{s_0+\alpha/2,\ s_f+\alpha,\ 2\}-\epsilon.
\]
Here \(u_0=0\) belongs to every spectral Sobolev space, while the largest
forcing regularity available is \(s_f=0\). Thus \(p=\alpha-\epsilon\).

Our more specific estimate \(h^\alpha/J\) is compatible with that theorem:
\[
\frac{h^\alpha/J}{h^{\alpha-\epsilon}}=\frac{h^\epsilon}{J}\to0.
\]
The theorem is an upper bound for a class of data. It does not assert
that every member of that class has an observed slope exactly \(\alpha\).

The manuscript also contains a rational-error bound for its specified
rational construction. The production code here uses the positive BRASIL
inverse representation with a constant term. Its rational order and error
should not be identified with that particular theorem's rational term
without an additional approximation argument. The current BRASIL error
was checked independently against exact fractional rates on the tested cases.

# Temporal error, rational error, and the diffusion parameter

The triangle inequality gives
\[
\big|\|u-U_{h,m}^{\tau}\|-\|u-u_h\|\big|
\leq\|u_h-U_{h,m}^{\tau}\|.
\]
Splitting the right-hand side into temporal and rational contributions
explains what must be small before a spatial slope can be interpreted.

A sufficient asymptotic strategy is to take temporal and rational errors
\(o(h^\alpha/J)\). Keeping a small \(\tau\) and a sufficiently accurate
rational approximation fixed instead gives only a finite interval of
spatial-dominant meshes. That is the strategy validated here.

## What diffusion changes

The rates are \(a_j=\nu\mu_j^{\alpha/2}\). For high modes,
\[
a_JT\approx\nu T\pi^\alpha h^{-\alpha}.
\]
The approximation \(F(a_J,T)\approx T\), used in the spatial-tail
asymptotics, requires this quantity to be large.

Smaller \(\nu\) makes the dynamics less stiff and can permit a larger
time step. It also moves the onset of high-frequency relaxation toward
finer meshes. Therefore reducing diffusion is not automatically an
improvement for observing the same spatial asymptotic over a fixed mesh range.

For example, with \(\alpha=0.5\), \(\nu=10^{-3}\), and \(T=1\), the condition
\(a_JT\gg1\) approximately requires
\[
h\ll\pi(\nu T)^{1/\alpha}\approx3.1\times10^{-6}.
\]
That is much finer than the displayed mesh range.

The final comparison uses \(\nu=1\) for all curves. A separate diffusion
scaling was evaluated during validation and retained in the private
development records. Diffusion is fixed along each \(h\)-refinement curve;
varying it with \(h\) would change the physical problem during the
convergence study.

## What rational order changes

At a discrete eigenvalue \(\lambda_h\), the rational evolution is backward
Euler with the effective positive rate
\[
\widehat a_h
=\frac{\nu\kappa^\alpha}
{\mathcal R_m(\lambda_h/\kappa^2)}.
\]
Its steady solution on that component is proportional to
\(\mathcal R_m(\lambda_h/\kappa^2)\). Thus a rational approximation error
can persist in time rather than averaging away.

The main run uses \(m=14\). The validation reruns the finest mesh with
\(m=12\), keeping the same time step, and separately compares the order-14
rates with exact fractional rates. The latter comparison is important:
a small change between two approximations alone would not prove that
both approximations are accurate.

# A complete pass through the code

## Loading definitions

`load.R` sources `problem.R`, `matrix_solver.R`, `experiment.R`, and
`plotting.R`. It does not run a convergence case, read credentials, send a
notification, or compile the C++ code.

The experiment is designed to be called from the project root. This note's
setup detects that root and sources the definitions using absolute paths.

## rough_mesh(J, kappa)

Its operations, in order, are:

1. Validate the refinement level and positive shift.
2. Construct the graph drawing.
3. Select the compatible `MetricGraph` constructor. The current and older
   APIs accept different input forms.
4. Set physical edge lengths to exactly 1 and 2.
5. Build the uniform mesh and assemble \(C,G,K\).
6. Check dimensions and element lengths.
7. Find and sort loop interior nodes using `PtE`.
8. Form the resolved index vector `j <- seq_len(J-1L)`.
9. Assemble the analytic load columns \(B_j\) and then \(b\).
10. Return matrices, graph metadata, indices, coordinates, and parameters.

The matrix `B` has zero-initialized stem and junction rows. Only loop
interior rows need explicit sine–hat entries. In `outer(x, 2^j, ...)`,
rows correspond to spatial nodes and columns to selected modes.
The repeated factor in `rep(..., each=length(loop))` multiplies every
entry of a column by that column's sinc-squared load factor.

## rough_projection(mesh)

It factors \(C\), solves \(CP=B\), and builds \(\mathsf R_h\) from
elementwise residuals. `crossprod(residual)` means
\(\mathrm{residual}^\mathsf T\mathrm{residual}\). The factor \(h\) and
Gauss weights turn these pointwise residual products into integrals.
The function returns `P` and `residual_gram`.

## rough_rates(), rough_response_integral(), rough_tail()

These implement, respectively,
\[
a_j=\nu(\kappa^2+\pi^2 2^{2j})^{\alpha/2},\qquad
F(a,T),\qquad
\sum_{j\geq J}\frac{F(a_j,T)}{j^2a_j^2}
\]
with the stable branches and remainder bound already derived.

`rough_rates()` returns rates of the **continuous** modes.
Passing those rates to the C++ routine supplies exact-reference
coefficients for the error calculation. They are not the numerical FEM
evolution rates.

## rough_rational_coefficients(), rough_transfer(), rough_operator()

`rough_rational_coefficients()` extracts one exact exponent row from the
package table, checks finite values and positivity, and sorts the poles.
It does not interpolate between exponent rows.

`rough_transfer()` constructs the partial fractions of \(H_m\), checks
their signs, and verifies reconstruction.

`rough_operator()` forms the shifted matrices, stores the transformed
residues and constant term, and creates `Matrix` factorizations for the
R reference step.

## rough_matrix_step(operator, rhs)

This function directly evaluates
\[
dC^{-1}\mathrm{rhs}
+\sum_\ell w_\ell(K/\kappa^2-z_\ell C)^{-1}\mathrm{rhs}.
\]
It is useful for checking the compiled loop against the R matrix formulation.
It is not a scalar modal solver.

## rough_compile_solver()

`Rcpp::sourceCpp()` compiles `matrix_evolution.cpp` with RcppEigen and
exposes `rough_matrix_evolve_cpp()` to R. The function checks whether that
compiled R-callable function already exists before compiling.

It needs a C++ compiler for recomputation. Reading the saved result and
rendering the results notebook does not require compilation.

## rough_solve()

This function organizes one complete case:

1. Set \(N=\lceil T/\tau_{\mathrm{target}}\rceil\), then use the actual
   \(\tau=T/N\). This ends the grid at \(T\).
2. Build the exact symmetry restriction if enabled.
3. Compute the restricted continuum projection and check that its lift is \(P\).
4. Build the rational operator for the actual \(\tau\).
5. Compute the infinite unresolved tail independently of time stepping.
6. Convert sparse matrices to a general compressed-column representation
   accepted by the Eigen interface.
7. Call the C++ matrix time loop.
8. Lift the final state, and any requested saved states, to the full graph.
9. Return error components, timing, actual step count, order, tail metadata,
   and the partial-fraction reconstruction discrepancy.

The `elapsed` field times the compiled call, including its own factorization
work. It excludes earlier graph construction, R-side factorizations,
projection setup, and tail setup.

The compiled function creates Eigen factorizations from the explicit
matrices. It does not reuse R's CHOLMOD factor objects; the two libraries
have different factor representations. This duplicates some one-time
setup but does not refactor matrices at every time step.

## The C++ loop, line by line in mathematical terms

The routine begins by checking dimensions. It factors the mass matrix and
every shifted matrix using `Eigen::SimplicialLDLT`. The factors are stored
in `unique_ptr` objects because these factorization objects are not
intended to be copied as ordinary values.

It precomputes the fixed quantities
\[
d_j,\qquad 1-\omega(a_j\tau),\qquad V(a_j\tau).
\]

For each integer \(k=1,\ldots,N\):

1. `rhs = C*u + tau*load` forms \(C U^{k-1}+\tau b\).
2. `next = remainder*mass_factor.solve(rhs)` evaluates the constant term.
3. The loop over residues adds every shifted sparse solve.
4. `u.swap(next)` makes the new vector current, reusing storage.
5. With \(t_0=(k-1)\tau\), it evaluates the exact coefficient means and
   the sum of their interval variances.
6. `delta = u - projection*mean` forms the projected coefficient difference.
7. `value` is the nonnegative resolved interval contribution
   \[
   \tau[\delta^\mathsf TC\delta+\bar c^\mathsf T\mathsf R_h\bar c+
   \mathrm{variance\_sum}].
   \]
8. It rejects a nonfinite or negative contribution.
9. It adds this contribution using compensated summation.
10. It saves the vector only if `return_states=TRUE`.

The expression `(k & 4095)==0` tests every 4096th iteration and allows
an R user interrupt. It does not skip any steps.

`noalias()` tells Eigen that the left-hand side does not overlap the
input expressions. The separate `u`, `rhs`, and `next` buffers support this
assumption and avoid unnecessary temporaries.

At the end the function returns
\[
\mathrm{error}=\sqrt{\mathrm{resolved\_squared}+\mathrm{tail\_squared}}.
\]
The zero-based C++ vector index \(0\) corresponds to mathematical mode
\(j=1\). The separate `mode_j` vector supplies the actual mathematical \(j\),
so the amplitude is \(1/(j a_j)\), not \(1/(0a_j)\).

## Why compensated summation is used

There can be up to five million positive interval contributions. Ordinary
summation can repeatedly lose small increments once the running sum has
grown. The code carries a compensation:
\[
\begin{aligned}
y&=\mathrm{value}-c,\\
t&=\mathrm{total}+y,\\
c&=(t-\mathrm{total})-y,\\
\mathrm{total}&=t.
\end{aligned}
\]
This reduces accumulation rounding error. It does not eliminate errors
inside sparse solves, coefficient evaluation, or quadrature.

## rough_parameters() and rough_run_experiment()

The parameters specify five meshes and eight values
\[
\alpha=0.5,0.7,0.9,1.1,1.3,1.5,1.7,1.9.
\]
The time step is fixed along each spatial refinement curve, but differs
between curves to keep temporal contamination small.

`expand.grid(J=..., alpha_index=...)` makes \(J\) vary fastest.
R fills matrices column by column, so reshaping the returned scalar errors
puts meshes in rows and alpha values in columns. The expression
`corrected <- errors * parameters$J` scales each row by its own \(J\),
using R's column-major recycling over the entire matrix.

Each case can run independently. On Unix, `mclapply()` distributes complete
cases over fork workers. This is computational parallelism, not a different
numerical method. Worker errors are caught and propagated to the caller.

A checkpoint includes its parameters and MD5 fingerprints of the R/C++
helper files. A checkpoint with a different identity is rejected. Thus old
curves are not silently mixed with new parameter choices or source versions.

Before saving compact case summaries, the driver removes `final_state`
and `states`. The complete results contain parameters, error matrices,
rates, per-case metadata, source fingerprints, generation time, and session
information.

## Plotting and the presentation notebook

`rough_convergence_plot()` expands the same mesh/alpha layout as the
calculation. It plots raw \(E\) or corrected \(JE\), using logarithmic axes.

The dashed raw model is \(A_\alpha h^\alpha/J\), and the dashed corrected
model is \(A_\alpha h^\alpha\). For either model, the vertical constant is
the geometric mean of error/model ratios over the fitted meshes:
\[
A_\alpha=\exp\left(\frac1{\#\mathcal F}
\sum_{J\in\mathcal F}\log\frac{E_J}{\mathrm{model}_J}\right).
\]
The dashed slopes are prescribed by the model. They are not fitted slopes
disguised as theoretical predictions. The observed slopes are calculated
separately by `lm()`.

`rough_save_figures()` saves both PNG and PDF versions.
`conv_in_h_rough.Rmd` reads the completed result, checks its parameter
identity, and displays the final figures and tables. It does not rerun
the matrix evolution while rendering.

# A small worked example: \(J=4\)

Here \(h=1/16\), \(n=16\), and the full graph has 48 nodes.
The quarter-loop has \(16/2-1=7\) unknowns.

The exact forcing load uses only
\[
j=1,2,3,\qquad k_j=2,4,8.
\]
It is
\[
b=B_1+\frac12B_2+\frac13B_3.
\]
All \(j\geq4\) loads vanish. However, all of those modes remain in
\(E_{\mathrm{tail}}^2\). The highest resolved angular cell frequency is
\(\theta_3=\pi/2\).

The following example is deliberately not evaluated when rendering this
note; it shows how to request full states for a small verification case.

```{r worked-example, eval=FALSE, echo=TRUE}
library(Matrix)
source("fun/rough/load.R")
rough_compile_solver(cache_dir = tempdir())
mesh <- rough_mesh(J = 4L, kappa = 4)
projection <- rough_projection(mesh, quadrature_order = 16L)

reduced <- rough_solve(
  mesh, alpha = 1.3, time_step = 0.002, order = 14L,
  diffusion = 1, T_final = 0.1, projection = projection,
  return_states = TRUE, symmetry_reduction = TRUE, coefficient_source = "brasil")

full <- rough_solve(
  mesh, alpha = 1.3, time_step = 0.002, order = 14L,
  diffusion = 1, T_final = 0.1, projection = projection,
  return_states = TRUE, symmetry_reduction = FALSE, coefficient_source = "brasil")

max(abs(reduced$states - full$states))
reduced$error
reduced$tail
```

The expected agreement concerns the **lifted full FEM vectors at every
time step**, not just similarity of final regression slopes.

# Current settings and saved results

These tables are loaded from the saved result rather than retyped.
The result was generated at `r saved$generated_at`.

```{r final-settings}
settings <- data.frame(alpha = parameters$alpha,
  target_tau = format(parameters$time_steps, scientific = TRUE, digits = 7),
  m = parameters$rational_order, nu = parameters$diffusion)
knitr::kable(settings, col.names = c("alpha", "Target tau", "m", "nu"))
```

The actual count and step from the finest mesh are:

```{r actual-steps}
finest <- Filter(function(x) x$J == max(parameters$J), saved$cases)
steps <- do.call(rbind, lapply(finest, function(x) data.frame(
  alpha = x$alpha, N = x$N, actual_tau = format(x$tau, scientific = TRUE, digits = 7),
  full_nodes = x$n_nodes, solver_nodes = x$n_solver_nodes,
  tail_last_j = x$tail$last_j)))
knitr::kable(steps)
```

```{r final-rates}
knitr::kable(saved$rates, digits = c(1, 1, 4, 4, 2),
  col.names = c("alpha", "Reference", "Raw slope", "Corrected slope", "Relative error (%)"))
```

The percentages in the last column concern corrected **regression slopes**.
They are not relative errors of the numerical solution.

## What the independent validation establishes

The development record is
[VALIDATION.md](../../DOCS/NAP/rough_experiment/all_alphas/VALIDATION.md).
Its files are separate from the results notebook. The recorded checks include:

- Independent local assembly of the full mass and stiffness matrices.
- Numerical hat integrations checking resolved loads and vanishing high-mode loads.
- Doubling residual quadrature order.
- Tighter tail summation compared with the geometric remainder.
- Every-step agreement with the original full R matrix solver, for all eight alpha values.
- A direct independent space–time integral of a small FEM solution.
- A 55-digit spectral calculation compared with all forty reported errors.
- Actual finest-mesh matrix runs with half the time step.
- Actual finest-mesh matrix runs at rational order 12.

The full-matrix versus reduced compiled iterate discrepancy in the recorded
core fixtures was at most approximately \(4.17\times10^{-16}\).
The direct integral agreed at approximately \(2.37\times10^{-16}\) relative error.
Across all forty cases, the high-precision comparison had maximum relative
norm discrepancy approximately \(3.51\times10^{-6}\).
The independent temporal solution error was at most \(3.08\%\) of the ideal
spatial error, and the rational solution error was at most \(0.040\%\).

The actual time-step-halving changes of the finest-mesh total error were
at most \(0.067\%\), and the order-12 versus order-14 changes were at most
\(0.047\%\). These are different quantities from the auxiliary solution-error
ratios above.

The spectral oracle uses the explicit uniform-mesh identities in the rate
analysis and evaluates geometric time sums in high precision. It is an
independent verification of the matrix algorithm, not the algorithm used
to generate the published curves. Its finite high-frequency sum runs
through mode 99; the same geometric tail estimate makes the remaining
part negligible for the tested alpha values. High precision reduces
cancellation in the oracle; it does not turn package coefficient rows,
which originate as floating-point data, into exact minimax coefficients.

# How to reproduce or change the experiment

The main run can be started from the project root with:

```{r reproduce, eval=FALSE, echo=TRUE}
library(Matrix)
source("fun/rough/load.R")
p <- readRDS("data_files/rough_comparison/brasil_h_results.rds")$parameters
p$coefficient_source <- "brasil"
result <- rough_run_experiment(
  parameters = p,
  checkpoint_dir = "/tmp/rough-h-checkpoints",
  workers = 3L,
  cache_dir = "/tmp/rough-rcpp-cache")
rough_save_figures(result)
```

The verified development environment uses `/usr/bin/Rscript --vanilla`,
R 4.5.2. The shell's default R may point to another version and package
library. This is why a rendering or recomputation command should use the
installation with the required packages. No global R environment change
is needed.

The dependency roles are:

| Dependency | Role |
|---|---|
| Matrix | Sparse FEM matrices and R reference factorizations |
| MetricGraph | Metric graph and full FEM assembly |
| sp | Compatibility input for the older MetricGraph constructor |
| rSPDE | Positive BRASIL coefficient tables |
| statmod | Spatial Gauss–Legendre quadrature |
| Rcpp and RcppEigen | Compiled sparse matrix evolution |
| ggplot2 | Final convergence figures |
| knitr and rmarkdown | Tables, source display, and notebook rendering |

Changing \(\alpha\) requires a supported coefficient-table exponent.
Changing \(J\) preserves the analysis only with aligned dyadic meshes.
Changing the forcing or initial condition can invalidate both the vanished
high-mode loads and the quarter-loop symmetry. Changing \(\nu\), \(T\),
\(\tau\), or \(m\) requires new auxiliary-error checks.
Changing the time reconstruction changes the norm formula.

If a finite forcing is wanted instead, choose it explicitly and state that
it is a different experiment. At sufficiently fine meshes, a fixed finite
sum is smooth and can recover a second-order spatial slope.

# Common mistakes this construction avoids

| Mistake | Why it changes or invalidates the calculation |
|---|---|
| Treating \(\phi_j\) as the full ordered graph spectrum | The dyadic family is only a selected orthonormal subset |
| Checking only the edgewise eigenvalue equation | The vertex continuity and Kirchhoff conditions are part of the operator domain |
| Calling \(\dot H^s\) a mean-zero space | Here it is a shifted spectral Sobolev space |
| Replacing the forcing by sampled nodal values | High-frequency functions can vanish at every node but still have nonzero \(L_2\) energy |
| Omitting modes whose FEM loads vanish from the error | They are the source of the lower spatial-error bound |
| Replacing \(C^{-1}K\) by \(K\) inside a fractional power | They are different operators in coefficient coordinates |
| Using an ordinary vector norm | It is not the graph \(L_2\) norm |
| Dropping the rational constant term | It changes the backward Euler update |
| Using table exponent \(\alpha\) instead of \(\alpha/2\) | It approximates the wrong fractional power |
| Interpreting internal `operator$m` as the published rational degree | It is an old-loop compatibility count |
| Computing \(I-P^\mathsf TCP\) by subtraction for tiny residuals | It can lose relative accuracy and positivity |
| Computing \(\omega(2z)-\omega(z)^2\) directly for tiny \(z\) | It subtracts nearly equal numbers to obtain a quadratic-small result |
| Describing every numerical evaluation as exact | Stable Gaussian quadrature and floating-point arithmetic remain present |
| Applying quarter-loop symmetry to arbitrary data | The restricted subspace need not contain their solution |
| Claiming fixed \(\tau,m\) give \(h^\alpha/J\) for all \(h\to0\) | Temporal and rational floors eventually dominate |
| Applying the \(h^\alpha/J\) model at \(\alpha=2\) | The resolved low modes instead supply a dominant \(h^2\) term |
| Treating three regression points as a proof of the asymptotic exponent | The proof and the finite-range observations are separate pieces of evidence |
